opus-5.5.text:
Scaling up for us happens on a few dimensions at once, and they all have to move together.

The first is technology. We made a bet years ago that inference would become the dominant AI workload, and that it needed a fundamentally different architecture than training. Training is a compute problem; inference, especially generative inference, is a memory bandwidth problem. That's why we built around digital in-memory compute: putting compute right where the data lives so you're not constantly moving weights back and forth. Scaling the technology means taking that core insight and keeping it ahead as models get bigger, context windows get longer, and people want lower latency and more interactive, agentic use cases. So we're always thinking about the next generation of silicon, packaging, memory integration, and how chips talk to each other at rack scale.

The second is software, which people often underestimate. Great hardware nobody can easily use doesn't go anywhere. Customers want to take a model off the shelf, drop it onto our platform, and have it just work with the frameworks they already use. A big part of scaling is investing heavily in the compiler, the runtime, and the tooling so the experience is seamless.

The third is go-to-market and the ecosystem. A startup can't scale alone in this industry. You need foundry partners, memory and packaging partners, server OEMs, and cloud and enterprise customers willing to deploy at volume. Getting from a great proof of concept to thousands of cards in production data centers is a whole different muscle: supply chain, manufacturing, quality, support. That's where a lot of hardware companies stumble, so we've been very deliberate about building that operational capability.

And finally, people and capital. You have to keep attracting great engineers, and you need enough runway to get through multiple product generations, because this is a long game.

Underneath it all, what gives me confidence is that the market has come to us. When we started, people asked, "Why focus on inference?" Now everyone sees that inference is where the cost and energy pressure is, and that the economics of serving these models have to come down dramatically. If we keep executing on performance per watt and cost per token, the demand is there. The job now is to execute.

r001.rationale: The response says the scaling dimensions must move together and describes expanding from proof of concept to thousands of cards in production data centers, alongside manufacturing and support capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about it in a few layers. The first thing people get wrong about a chip company is they think the chip is the product. It's not. The chip is table stakes. What you're actually building is a platform — silicon, the interconnect, the software stack, the compiler, the runtime, the integration into the data center. If any one of those pieces is weak, the whole thing doesn't scale, no matter how good your silicon is. So a big part of scaling for us has been resisting the temptation to just be a silicon company and instead building out the full stack from day one.

The second piece is focus. We made a very deliberate bet early on that inference was going to be the big market, not training. When we started, that was contrarian — everyone was obsessed with training because that's where all the headlines were. But if you look at where the dollars go over time, inference is where you serve every user, every query, every token, and it has to be economical. So we built the architecture around that, around in-memory compute, around low latency for generative models, rather than trying to be a general-purpose part that does everything okay and nothing great. Scaling, for a startup, is really about saying no to a lot of things so you can be the best at one.

Then there's the ecosystem question. We're not going to beat the incumbents by replicating their ecosystem. We scale by being open — supporting standard frameworks, working with partners on the software side, making it so a customer doesn't have to rewrite their world to use us. If adopting your product is painful, you don't scale, period.

And honestly, the last piece is people and capital. Building silicon is capital intensive and the cycles are long — you're making bets today that pay off in two, three years. So you need investors who understand that, and you need a team that has done this before and knows where the bodies are buried. A lot of what I spend my time on is making sure we have the right people in the right seats, because the technology roadmap is only as good as the team executing it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses building a full-stack platform, partner adoption, and team and capital needs, but does not say that manufacturing, product deployment, and customer support must expand simultaneously.

astra-6.text:
I think about scaling on a few different levels. First, you have to deliver a product that solves a real customer problem. For us, that means making AI inference more efficient and economical. It’s not enough to have an interesting chip; the software and the overall system have to make it easy for customers to deploy and use.

Then you have to build the organization around that product. You need the right people, manufacturing and supply-chain partners, and the ability to support customers as they move from evaluating the technology to running it in production.

And you have to sequence those investments carefully. Hardware takes time and capital, so you need a long-term roadmap while staying focused on execution today. Ultimately, scaling means turning the technology into something customers can depend on, and then doing that repeatedly.

r001.rationale: The response mentions manufacturing, customer deployment, and customer support, but does not say they must expand simultaneously; it instead says to sequence investments carefully.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about scaling on a few levels. First, we have to deliver a product that solves a real customer problem. For AI inference, that means looking at the whole system—performance, power, cost, and how easily customers can deploy it—not just the chip.

Then we have to make that repeatable. Can we take what works with an early customer and deploy it across many customers without a lot of custom engineering? That makes software and the developer experience incredibly important.

And finally, there’s the organization: building the team and the partnerships to manufacture, deliver, and support the product. Those pieces have to scale together. Great technology gets you started, but reliably delivering value to customers is what lets you build a company.

r001.rationale: The response says the team and partnerships must scale to “manufacture, deliver, and support the product” and that “those pieces have to scale together,” covering manufacturing, deployment, and customer support expanding simultaneously.
